newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO sets date for enlargement summit.
newsitem.headline: NATO sets date for enlargement summit.

text.p: NATO fixed a date on Tuesday for an historic summit to invite former communist enemies to join the alliance, but sought to deflect Russian anger by pledging not to station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.

Foreign ministers of the 16 allies, bound together in the most powerful military alliance ever assembled, said they would hold a summit next July 8 and 9 at which some countries from central and eastern Europe would be invited to begin accession talks.
"The decisions taken at that summit will not only shape NATO for the next generation, but will also shape Europe," said one senior official. The summit will be held in Madrid.

Negotiations and ratification by current member states could take up to two years, but the aim is to have the first new members for more than two decades inside the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) by its 50th anniversary in 1999.
Russia bitterly opposes NATO's plans, saying it risks creating new dividing lines in Europe.

In an attempt to lessen that opposition while emphasising enlargement was non-negotiable, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said the alliance had no plans to station nuclear weapons on the territory of Moscow's former allies.

"In today's Europe NATO has no intention, no plan and no need to station nuclear weapons on the territory of any new members," Christopher said at the start of a two-day meeting of alliance foreign ministers.
Officials said the ministers had also decided to start work on drawing up a shortlist from 11 countries now clamouring to join the alliance.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are currently favourites to be first through the door possibly with Slovenia and Romania.

NATO is keen to match the enlargement process with a dialogue with Russia culminating in a comprehensive charter governing all aspects of the relationship between the two former Cold War foes which would also be signed at the July summit.
"Next year's summit will mark the moment when the processes of transformation and change converge and the new Alliance takes stock," NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said.
But so far Moscow has rebuffed all NATO's attempts to get to the negotiating table and has shown no sign of lessening its virulent opposition to enlargement.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the alliance now had to step up efforts to bring Russia to the negotiating table.
"We now have six months, this is enough, but we will really have to get going, we have to get there now," he told reporters.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was expected to arrive in Brussels later on Tuesday to attend the second day of the two-day meeting.

Alliance foreign ministers are likely to push him strongly to start negotiations and agree to the exchange of military liasion officers, stressing the enlargement timetable has now been irreversibly set in motion.
But shortly before he left for Brussels, Russia dismissed suggestions it had changed its position as "fantasy".
"Russia's position on this issue remains firm and rather tough," President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a briefing.

"It has not changed although our partners in dialogue have tried at various times to send to the world other signals... that Moscow has started to look more flexible, as if it had internally accepted such expansion. No. That is all fantasy."

NATO foreign ministers also reviewed plans to transform the alliance's command structures to enable it to carry out more Bosnia-style peacekeeping missions and to boost cooperation programmes with other non-NATO countries.
Several allies are concerned that countries, such as the Baltic states which are not likely to gain NATO membership in the "first wave", should be offered the possibility of closer ties.
